passage_title: The Day's Fish
passage:
[1] I got the job at Hanlon's Fish because my bus stopped in front of it and because, on the afternoon I walked in to ask, Mrs. Hanlon was alone behind the counter with a line out the door and a halibut on the scale. "Can you count change backward?" she said, and when I said I could, she handed me an apron that had been washed so many times the lettering on it read only "ANLON." I was sixteen. I believed I had been hired for my competence, and it was some weeks before I understood I had been hired for being there.

[2] The shop was three generations old and smelled like it: ice, lemon, the bleach the floor was mopped with at closing, and under all of it the sea, which no amount of bleach reached. Mrs. Hanlon's father had opened it to sell what the boats out of the harbor brought in. Mrs. Hanlon still bought from two of those boats, and from a truck that came up from the city on Tuesdays and Fridays, and she could tell you which fish in the case had come from where without looking at the tags.

[3] I could not. For the first month everything on the ice looked to me equally like fish. She taught me the way she did everything, in a sentence and then in silence. Press the flesh, she said, and watch whether it comes back. Look at the eye, not the skin; skin can be made to shine. Then she let me get it wrong in front of her for weeks without saying another word about it, which I found unbearable then and which I now think was the only way anyone could have taught it.

[4] What I learned faster was the other thing she did, which embarrassed me. When a customer pointed at something on the ice, Mrs. Hanlon would sometimes say, "Not that one today." She said it pleasantly, in the voice she used for the weather, and then she would point them to something else, usually something cheaper. I had worked out within a week what this cost her. The fish she steered people away from had been paid for. It sat on the ice until it was too old to sell and then it went into the bucket for the man who made chowder for the diner across the street, at a price that I calculated, privately and with indignation, came to about a third of what she had paid.

[5] So on a Saturday in July, with Mrs. Hanlon in the back on the telephone with one of the boats, I sold the sole. A woman asked about it and I did not say "Not that one today." I said it was lovely, which was a word I had heard Mrs. Hanlon use, and I wrapped two pounds of it and took her money and felt, ringing it up, the way I imagine a bookkeeper feels who has found a mistake in someone else's arithmetic and quietly put it right.

[6] Mrs. Hanlon came out while I was still at the register. She looked at the gap on the ice and then at me, and she did not ask. She went to the bulletin board by the door and took down a card with the woman's name and telephone number on it; the woman had been coming in since before I was born. Then she went back to the office and closed the door, and I heard her voice through it, low and even, and I heard the word "sole."

[7] She did not mention it to me that day or afterward. On Monday the woman came in and Mrs. Hanlon gave her a piece of halibut and would not take money for it, and the woman laughed and said she had cooked the sole anyway and it had been fine, really, a little soft, and Mrs. Hanlon said that fine was not what she sold. Neither of them looked at me, and I have thought since that this was a courtesy and not a punishment, though it took me most of the summer to tell the difference.

[8] I worked at Hanlon's for three summers. In the last of them I said "Not that one today" for the first time, to a man pointing at a tray of scallops, and I heard my voice come out exactly level, the way hers did, as if I were reporting rain. He bought the cod instead. I watched him go and did the arithmetic on the scallops without meaning to, and found that the number no longer felt like a loss, though it was exactly the same number it had always been.

choices: the harbor boats her father had dealt with, though she now buys from every boat that comes in.
two of the harbor boats and a truck that came up from the city twice a week.
a city truck that had replaced the harbor boats once the shop passed to her.
the harbor boats in season and the city truck during the months they stayed in.
correct_answer: two of the harbor boats and a truck that came up from the city twice a week.
explanation: Paragraph 2 says Mrs. Hanlon "still bought from two of those boats, and from a truck that came up from the city on Tuesdays and Fridays" - two boats plus a twice-weekly truck. The word "still" means the truck did not replace the boats, and the paragraph limits her to "two of those boats," not every boat. Nothing divides the year into a boat season and a truck season; both sources are named together without any reference to months.

an instance of something happening.
a matter to be decided in a court.

prompt: In paragraph 7, the narrator's view of the moment when "Neither of them looked at me" is that it was:
choices: a kindness that kept her out of an exchange that could only have shamed her.

passage_title: Greening the Vacant Lot: Two Views
passage:
Passage A

[1] For most of the last century, a vacant lot in an American city was treated as an absence: a place where a building used to be and where, with luck, another one would be someday. Cities fenced some of them, mowed a few, and otherwise left them to collect what vacant lots collect. Philadelphia, which by the 2010s had tens of thousands of them, began asking a different question. What if the lot itself, and not the building it was waiting for, was doing something to the block?

[2] The question was put to a test of an unusually strict kind. Researchers working with the city and a local horticultural society took several hundred vacant lots and assigned them by chance to one of three treatments. Some were "greened": cleared of trash and debris, planted with grass and a few trees, and edged with a low wooden fence that made them look tended without closing them off. Some were only cleaned of trash. The rest were left as they were. Because chance, in effect, decided which lot got which treatment, any difference that later appeared between the groups could not be put down to the city having chosen the most promising blocks.

[3] Differences appeared. In the neighborhoods below the poverty line, gun violence around the greened lots fell by roughly a third relative to the lots left alone, and residents near them reported feeling safer outdoors. The cleanup-only lots showed smaller and less consistent changes. And the researchers found no sign that the decline had simply reappeared a few blocks over, which is what skeptics of place-based crime policy usually expect: crime pushed around rather than prevented.

[4] The cost is what makes the result hard to ignore. A greened lot costs on the order of a thousand dollars or so to create and a modest sum each year to keep mowed. Very little else that a city can do about violence can be bought at that price, and almost nothing else has been tested this way. The researchers offered several explanations: that an abandoned lot is a convenient place to hide a weapon; that a tended one tells everyone passing that someone is paying attention; that people who use a space become its watchers. They did not claim to know which one was doing the work.

Passage B

[1] I do not doubt the Philadelphia numbers, and I would rather see a vacant lot mowed than not. My hesitation is about what a result like that becomes once it leaves the paper it was published in. A trial answers the question it was designed to answer. This one asked whether a particular treatment, applied by a particular organization in a particular city, changed what happened on the surrounding blocks over a particular period. It did. What it was not designed to answer is the question a city council will actually ask, which is whether greening will do the same thing on their blocks, under their budget, a decade from now.

[2] That gap matters because nobody knows why the lots worked. If the mechanism is that weapons can no longer be hidden in the weeds, then any thorough cleanup should help, and the fence and the grass are decoration. If it is that a neighborhood reads care in a tended lot, then the care has to keep arriving, and a program that is funded for three years and mowed for two may teach the opposite lesson. These are not the same policy, and an average effect cannot tell you which one you are buying.

[3] There is also the matter of who the improvement is for. Planners have a name, green gentrification, for what can happen when a poor neighborhood acquires parks and gardens: the blocks become more attractive, rents rise, and the residents the greenery was meant to serve find they cannot afford to stay and enjoy it. A greened lot is a small thing, and one lot will not reprice a neighborhood. A citywide program of them is not a small thing.

[4] None of this is an argument for leaving lots to the weeds. It is an argument for asking the people who live beside them what they want done, and for building into any program the one thing a trial cannot supply: a commitment that outlasts the study.

passage:
Passage A

[1] For most of the last century, a vacant lot in an American city was treated as an absence: a place where a building used to be and where, with luck, another one would be someday. Some were only cleaned of trash. The rest were left as they were. passage_title: Staves of Unequal Width
passage:
[1] A barrel is held together by nothing but its own shape. There is no glue in it and, in a well-made one, no nail; thirty-odd oak staves stand edge to edge inside iron hoops, and the hoops, driven down toward the barrel's swollen middle, squeeze the staves against one another until the joints close tight enough to hold wine for years. Every part of the vessel is pushing on every other part. Take off the hoops and it falls into a heap of curved boards that look as though they could never have held water.

[2] I spent a winter watching Ruth Abele make and mend barrels in a shed behind a winery, and the first thing she corrected was my assumption that the staves were identical. They are not, and in a hand-made barrel they cannot be. Oak is split or sawn from logs of whatever width the tree allowed, and a cooper who insisted on staves of one width would waste most of the wood. So the staves in any barrel vary, some nearly twice as wide as others, and the cooper's work is to make unequal pieces close into a circle.

[3] The work happens at the edges. Each stave is shaped wider at its middle and narrower at its ends, and each long edge is planed to an angle so that it will meet its neighbor flat when the staves lean together. That angle is not the same on a wide stave as on a narrow one, and Abele did not measure it. She ran each edge along a long plane fixed upside down on a bench, sighted down it, ran it again. When I asked how she knew the angle was right, she held two staves together against the window and looked for light between them. "If the light comes through, the wine goes out," she said, and went back to the plane.

[4] It would be easy to tell this as a story about intuition, the knowing hand against the measuring mind, and I was tempted to tell it that way until Abele objected. Nothing she did was mysterious to her, she said. She could have worked out the angle in degrees for any stave I handed her; she simply had no need to, because the stave would tell her faster. The window test is a measurement, and a strict one. It is merely a measurement of the thing that matters, the closing of a joint, rather than of a number that is supposed to predict it.

[5] What took her years to learn, she said, was not the angle but the wood. An oak stave is not a uniform material. It bends more readily along some lengths than others; it may hold a knot that will not take the curve; it will move as it dries. When the staves are raised in a ring and their splayed ends are drawn together over a small fire, some yield and some fight, and a cooper who has learned only the geometry will crack a stave that a cooper who has learned the wood would have warmed a minute longer. No drawing could show her which. She learned it by cracking staves, as her teacher had.

[6] This is the part of the craft that is hardest to write down, and it is why apprenticeship once lasted as long as it did. The proportions of a barrel could be taught in an afternoon; the trade's old names for its parts and tools could be learned in a week. What took the years was the accumulation of particular cases: this grain, that knot, a stave from one side of a tree that bent unlike a stave from the other. Abele keeps no notes. She says the notes would be a list of exceptions, and that by the time she wrote one down the next barrel would offer a new one.

[7] Most barrels sold today are made with the help of machines, which cut staves to set widths and set angles from wood that has been graded to behave alike. Abele does not disapprove; the machines solve the problem of unequal wood by refusing to accept it. Her own work is mostly repair, and a repair is the one job the machine cannot do, because the barrel that comes into her shed has already settled its own shape, and the new stave must be made to fit what is there.

[1] A barrel is held together by nothing but its own shape. There is no glue in it and, in a well-made one, no nail; thirty-odd oak staves stand edge to edge inside iron hoops, and the hoops, driven down toward the barrel's swollen middle, squeeze the staves against one another until the joints close tight enough to hold wine for years. [2] I spent a winter watching Ruth Abele make and mend barrels in a shed behind a winery, and the first thing she corrected was my assumption that the staves were identical. They are not, and in a hand-made barrel they cannot be. Oak is split or sawn from logs of whatever width the tree allowed, and a cooper who insisted on staves of one width would waste most of the wood. So the staves in any barrel vary, some nearly twice as wide as others, and the cooper's work is to make unequal pieces close into a circle.

[3] The work happens at the edges. Each stave is shaped wider at its middle and narrower at its ends, and each long edge is planed to an angle so that it will meet its neighbor flat when the staves lean together. That angle is not the same on a wide stave as on a narrow one, and Abele did not measure it. She ran each edge along a long plane fixed upside down on a bench, sighted down it, ran it again. When I asked how she knew the angle was right, she held two staves together against the window and looked for light between them. "If the light comes through, the wine goes out," she said, and went back to the plane.

[4] It would be easy to tell this as a story about intuition, the knowing hand against the measuring mind, and I was tempted to tell it that way until Abele objected. passage_title: The Long Fall of Marine Snow

[1] Divers who descend below the sunlit surface of the open ocean often describe the same sight: a slow, endless drift of pale flecks through the beams of their lights, as if it were snowing underwater. Nearly all of it was built near the surface by microscopic algae, which draw carbon dioxide out of the water as they photosynthesize, the water in turn taking up more of the gas from the air. When the algae die or are eaten, some of that carbon begins to fall. Carbon that sinks far enough, below a depth of perhaps a thousand meters, can stay out of contact with the atmosphere for centuries or longer. Oceanographers call this downward transport the biological pump, and it is one reason the atmosphere holds less carbon dioxide than it otherwise would.

[3] The pump, however, leaks badly. A sinking flake is food, and it is eaten, broken apart, and digested by bacteria and animals all the way down. Most of the carbon that leaves the surface is returned to the water as dissolved carbon dioxide within the upper few hundred meters, where it can come back into contact with the air within years to decades. Only a small fraction reaches the deep sea, and a smaller fraction still settles on the seafloor. How fast a flake falls largely decides its fate. Small, loose particles may sink only a few meters a day and are consumed long before they get anywhere; dense fecal pellets and large aggregates can fall hundreds of meters a day and outrun much of the feeding.

[4] For decades the standard way to measure the pump was to hang cylinders called sediment traps at fixed depths and count what fell into them. But they also have a deeper limitation. They measure only what sinks, and not all of the carbon that travels downward does.

The usual explanation is that darkness protects them from predators that hunt by sight, so they feed at the surface only when they cannot be seen. A copepod that eats at the surface at midnight and descends at dawn carries carbon down in its gut and its tissues, and it releases that carbon at depth, by breathing, by excreting, and sometimes by dying there. None of this carbon falls; it is carried. A sediment trap, waiting for particles to drop into it, never records it at all.

They scatter from nets and avoid lights. Much of the recent progress has come from acoustic surveys, which detect the migrating layers by the echoes they return, and from instruments that drift with ocean currents and photograph particles as they pass. What the new tools have mostly shown is that the old picture of a single steady rain of particles was too simple: carbon reaches the deep ocean by several routes at once, some falling and some swimming.
